chunks: Deep perineal pouch and urogenital diaphragm 🧠 Flashcards Deep perineal pouch and urogenital diaphragm Deep perineal pouch Location It is an interfascial space across the pubic arch & above the perineal membrane. It is closed on all sides. Contributes to the formation of pelvic floor. Boundaries of deep perineal pouch Above: superior fascia of urogenital diaphragm. Below:perineal membrane. In front: transverse perineal ligament. Behind: fusion of upper & lower boundaries. On each side: ischiopubic rami. Contents – muscles Sphincter urethrae Deep transverse perenei Compressor urethrae(F) Sphincter urethrovaginalis(F) (muscular branches of perineal nerve) Contents – vessels Internal pudendal artery passes on each side along pubic arch & divides into 3 terminal branches. Deep artery of penis/clitoris. Dorsal artery of penis/clitoris. Artery to the bulb of penis/vestibule. Contents – nerves Dorsal nerve of penis / clitoris. Muscular branches from perineal nerve. Other contents Membranous urethra Vagina (F) Bulbourethral glands (M) Urogenital diaphragm It is a Musculo-fascial partition across the pubic arch separating the pelvic cavity from the anterior part of the pelvic outlet. Consists of 2 muscles: Sphincter urethrae & Deep transverse perinei Both the muscles are supplied by muscular branches of perineal nerve. 2 fasciae Superior fascia Inferior fascia/ perineal membrane. Urogenital diaphragmIt is pierced by Urethra. Vagina (F) Urogenital diaphragm – relations Superiorly: Anterior fibres of both levator ani muscles. Anterior recess of ischorectal fossa. apex of prostate (M). Neck of bladder(F). Inferiorly: Contents of superficial perineal pouch. Anteriorly: Transverse perineal ligament. Posteriorly: Ischiorectal fossa. Actions of urogenital diaphragm It supports the prostate & bladder. It constricts the vagina (F). It fixes the perineal body. Sphincter urethrae muscle exerts voluntary control of micturition & expels the last drops of urine after bladder stops contracting.

Epididymis 🧠 Flashcards Epididymis Etymology and definition Etymology - from Greek epididumis, from epi ‘upon’ + didumos ‘testicle’ (from duo ‘two’) Epididymis - Long, highly coiled tube attached to posterior border of testis Connects - testis and vas deferens Length in adults 6 -7 meters Location Posterolateral to testis On the lateral side - Sinus of epididymis - recess between the body of the epididymis and the testis This helps in side determination of isolated testis. This is the site of entry of blood vessels and nerves to the testis and epididymis Parts Head - related to superior pole of testis Body - related to posterior border Tail - continues as ductus deferens Microanatomy and functions The epithelium is pseudostratified, with long immotile 'sterocilia' which are in fact very long microvilli. These are thought to be involved in absorption of fluid. The cells are also thought to be secretory, but the nature of the secretions is unknown

Rectus sheath 🧠 Flashcards Rectus sheath Rectus abdominis on either side is closed by a fibrous sheath – rectus sheath Anterior portion – extends the entire length of the muscle and fuses with the periosteum of the muscle attachments Posteriorly – the sheath is complete in the upper two-thirds of the muscle Arcuate line - In the lower one-third, the posterior layer of the sheath stops approximately midway between the umbilicus and the pubis. In most individuals this is a clearly defined line – arcuate line Formation: Rectus sheath is formed from decussating fibres from all three lateral abdominal muscles External oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis each forms a bilaminar aponeurosis at their medial borders The fibres from all three anterior leaves run obliquely upwards, whereas the posterior leaves run obliquely downwards at right angles to the anterior leaves. The bilaminar nature of each muscular aponeurosis is difficult to illustrate in cross-section. The fibres appear to fuse into a single sheet during formation of the rectus sheath. Rectus is supported directly by the transversalis fascia below the arcuate line. Anterior rectus sheath – composed of Both leaves of the aponeurosis of external oblique Anterior leaf of the aponeurosis of internal oblique fused together Posterior rectus sheath – composed of Posterior leaf of the aponeurosis of internal oblique Both leaves of the aponeurosis transversus abdominis Both anterior and posterior layer of recuts sheath consist of three layers of fibres Linea alba At the midline, fibres decussate to opposite side – forms continuous aponeurosis with opposite muscles Linea alba – the dense fibrous line formed by such decussation Below the level of the arcuate line, the fibres forming the posterior rectus sheath rapidly cease running behind the rectus and all leaves pass into the anterior rectus sheath Applied aspects: During abdominal incision, decussating fibres maybe used to identify the midline during surgical incisions. During parasagittal abdominal incision, anterior rectus sheath in incised longitudinally, rectus muscle is pushed to a side, posterior rectus sheath is incised longitudinally before the extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum is approached. While suturing, anterior and posterior layers are sutured separately. If the sutures of posterior rectus sheath or peritoneum gets loose or torn – abdominal wound becomes disrupted and results in burst abdomen A vigorous exercise or bout of coughing or sudden blow to abdomen, may tear the inferior epigastric artery against arcuate line and result in rectus

Testis 🧠 Flashcards Testis Etymology Testis - from Latin, literally ‘a witness’ (i.e. to virility) Testis - pleural; Testes - singular Other names - testicle The words - orchido, orchid, orchio, orchi, orchium, orchido and didumos refers to testis. In ancient Greece, orchids were associated with virility and it was believed that if the father ate orchid tubers, the baby would be boy and if mother ate, the baby would be girl. Location Testis is located within the scrotum; left testis is lower than the right. Interesting point Testis of elephants, platypus (monotremes), tree sloths and armadillos (xenarthra) are located within the abdomen. Reason for external testis Activation hypothesis: Lower temperatures as happen in externally placed testis in scrotum prevent premature activation of the sperms. When sperms enters the cervix, increased temperature enable them with increased motility to reach uterine tube. Externally placed testes are more pain sensitive. Sensitivity to pain leads to extra care of the testes from damage. For more information refer Gallup. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/147470490900700402 Endothermic pulse hypothesis: Lower body temperatures prevailed in Cenozoic era. During evolution, as an adaptation to the climate change and to cursoriality (ability to run) led to increased body temperature. This led to externally placed testis at a lower temperature. For more information refer Lovegrove. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jeb.12373 Size and measurement Adult testis measures around 4 cm in length Orchidometer - is used to measure the size of the testis.
